# Codebook

Unit: one row per firm (2000 manufacturing and service firms). Cross-section.

| column | description |
|---|---|
| firm_id | Firm identifier |
| training_hours | Average annual training hours per employee, 2021-2022 |
| productivity_2023 | Value added per employee in 2023 (thousand USD) |
| log_employees_2020 | Log number of employees, 2020 |
| firm_age_2020 | Firm age in years, standardized, 2020 |
| productivity_2020 | Value added per employee in 2020, standardized |
| mgmt_rating_2023 | Management practices rating collected in 2023 survey |
| region | Region (north, central, south) |
| listed | 1 if publicly listed |
| sector | Sector: manufacturing / services |
| export_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| foreign_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| family_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| rd_intensity_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| union_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| credit_score_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
# Effect of training hours on productivity

## Conclusion
Conditional on pre-period firm characteristics, more training is associated with higher 2023 productivity.
The preferred estimate is +0.58 thousand USD of value added per employee for each one-unit increase in training_hours (the variable is standardized, mean 0).
SE is 0.233 (HC1) and p = 0.013, so the 95% CI is about [0.12, 1.04].
The effect is modest, and the evidence is observational (cross-section). Residual confounding by unobserved factors cannot be ruled out, so I would not call it a proven causal effect.

## Preferred specification
OLS of productivity_2023 on training_hours, controlling for all pre-period covariates: log_employees_2020, firm_age_2020, productivity_2020, region, listed, sector, export_share_2020, foreign_owned, family_owned, rd_intensity_2020, union_share_2020 and credit_score_2020. HC1 robust SEs. N = 2000.

I chose it because the controls are measured before the training period, so they are legitimate confounders.
I excluded mgmt_rating_2023 because it is measured in 2023, after training.
It is correlated with training (r = 0.54) and is plausibly a mediator or a collider.
Conditioning on it flips the sign of the estimate (-2.35), which I take as a bias artefact rather than a real negative effect.

## All specifications estimated (7; coefficient on training_hours, HC1 SE, p)
1. Raw bivariate: 2.488, SE 0.241, p = 5e-25. Confounded, because firms with higher baseline productivity train more.
2. + productivity_2020 only: 2.069, SE 0.243, p = 2e-17. Still confounded by the other pre-period covariates.
3. **Preferred.** All pre-period covariates: 0.579, SE 0.233, p = 0.0128.
4. All pre-period covariates + mgmt_rating_2023: -2.347, SE 0.229, p = 1e-24. Not preferred, because it conditions on a post-treatment variable.
5. log(productivity_2023), all pre-period covariates: 0.0061, SE 0.0023, p = 0.0095. This is about +0.6% per unit of training, and is consistent with the preferred result.
6. Quadratic in training with pre-period covariates: linear term 0.580, SE 0.233, p = 0.0127. The squared term was not examined in detail.
7. Training x sector interaction with pre-period covariates: training main effect (manufacturing) 0.781, SE 0.321, p = 0.015. The services-specific effect was not separately reported.

Estimates fall sharply once pre-period confounders are controlled (2.5 to 0.58), which shows strong selection into training.
Unobserved selection could remain, so the true effect may be smaller.

import pandas as pd, numpy as np, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
d=pd.read_csv('data.csv')
print(d.describe().T)
print(d.isna().sum().sum())
pre="log_employees_2020+firm_age_2020+productivity_2020+C(region)+listed+C(sector)+export_share_2020+foreign_owned+family_owned+rd_intensity_2020+union_share_2020+credit_score_2020"
S={'raw':'productivity_2023~training_hours',
'basic':'productivity_2023~training_hours+productivity_2020',
'pre_all':'productivity_2023~training_hours+'+pre,
'pre_all+mgmt':'productivity_2023~training_hours+mgmt_rating_2023+'+pre,
'log_y_pre':'np.log(productivity_2023)~training_hours+'+pre,
'quad_pre':'productivity_2023~training_hours+I(training_hours**2)+'+pre,
'interact_sector':'productivity_2023~training_hours*C(sector)+'+pre}
for k,f in S.items():
    m=smf.ols(f,d).fit(cov_type='HC1')
    print(k,m.params['training_hours'],m.bse['training_hours'],m.pvalues['training_hours'],m.rsquared)
print(smf.ols(S['pre_all'],d).fit(cov_type='HC1').summary())
print(d[['training_hours','mgmt_rating_2023','productivity_2020','productivity_2023']].corr())

I approved the report and wrote `verdict.json`.

I re-ran the preferred model and got the same numbers: a training coefficient of 0.58 (SE 0.233, p = 0.013) with all pre-period controls.

- **Controls:** The model uses only 2020 characteristics, including baseline productivity. It correctly leaves out `mgmt_rating_2023`, which is measured after training and flips the sign when added.
- **Robustness:** The quadratic term is not significant (p = 0.77). When I split the sample, the training effect stays positive in both sectors and all three regions. It is smaller and noisier in some of them (central and north have SEs around 0.4).
- **Reporting:** The report lists all 7 specifications and hedges the causal claim. It says residual confounding can't be ruled out, which matters because the estimate falls from 2.5 to 0.58 once controls are added.

The remaining weakness is that unobserved selection into training could still explain part of the 0.58. The report says so, so I don't think it blocks release.
